column2: BMC Community Bulletin (summer, No. I): “Molly Gregory’s Report on Community Work: 1942–1943” (chicks laying in the trees)
Special faculty meeting: Herbert Miller accuses Bentley of a lack of professional ethics (influencing students' choice of studies)
Faculty meeting: Bentley defends himself against the charge (Straus) of pro-Soviet indoctrination; a seven-point statement (“he is not a Communist… he writes for the Nation”)
Hansgirg and Straus find an old gold-mine shaft and mica in the pasture; faculty meeting: “eighteen people building castles in the air”
Special faculty meetings (August 16 and 17, 1943) and the provisional budget for the 11th year
The faculty decides to open “in good faith” in the fall: $17,000 in pledges, 55 enrolled (20-25 % boys); quicker passage to the senior division
Special meeting with the faculty (race relations)

Mid-October 1943: only one male student remains, Sam Brown (polio); the others leave with the last unit of the Enlisted Reserve Corps; no young American faculty members left (Lindsley, Evarts, Boyden, Mangold, Babcock, Jack French gone)
Board meeting on the mica
Faculty meeting (grades); Bentley's speech warning against rejecting “the discipline… of the older education” (supplement to BMC Bulletin No. 2, 1943-44)
Bentley stands up at lunch to toast the anniversary of the October Revolution of 1917
Stephen Duggar Jr. (Simpson, Thatcher & Bartlett) to Foreman: no North Carolina law requires segregation in higher education
Faculty meeting: the legal question of segregation
Alfred Kazin to Dreier (Dreier's reply on March 8, 1944)
Faculty meeting: a drunken fight between Jack Gilford and Archie McWilliams (a knife), McWilliams defended by de Graaff; Herbert Miller protests against “nude” sunbathing
James E. Shepard (North Carolina College for Negroes) to Wunsch: admitting Black students in the fall would do more harm than good
Faculty meeting: Wunsch's compromise: one to three chosen Black guests, as visitors, for three or four weeks at most, at the summer Music Institute; a course on race relations for the whole community

Regular and adjourned faculty meetings (April 19, May 3 and 10) and a special one (April 24): compromise: a single “qualified” Black woman admitted for the whole summer session as a “member of the Institute” (the “Hofjude,” according to Bentley); Straus “did not intend to fight”; a petition by 38 of the 50 students for more Black students
Josef Albers to René d'Harnoncourt (MoMA): also admit students “of the red and yellow races” to take away the decision's aggressive character
Resignation of the assistant treasurer Robert C. Orr (partly because of the admission of a Black student; “the-attempting-of-too-much-with-too-little disease”)
Wunsch to Junius Allison (then June 27, 1944); Wunsch to Evarts, May 6, 1944
Wunsch to Evarts: dress (“a lot of fat frying”); visit of the former student Jimmy Jamieson, who proposes “clothesless weekends”
Marine Lieutenant Allan T. Squire, a guest at the dance, writes the Board of Fellows a letter of protest (“your Black Mountain experiment die”)
Dreier to Forbes: the newcomers no longer share the “common ground”; Foreman leaves without raising funds
Wunsch to Forbes on the general meeting
Barbara (“Andy”) Anderson and Jeanne Wacker hitchhike north to visit Bentley at Fisk (having told Frances de Graaff); a night at the Highlander Folk School
Anderson and Wacker arrested by the police on the road to Chattanooga (“loitering”); a night in jail with prostitutes; Barbara Anderson turns 21 at midnight

Examination at the clinic (gonorrhea “diagnosed” in Anderson), court (the judge's sermon on the Scottsboro case, 60 days in the workhouse), questioning by the police chief, transfer to the county jail; a lawyer alerts the college; a telephone call to Dreier during the Music Institute
Dreier arrives in Chattanooga and obtains the suspension of the sentences on his promise to take them away; return by bus to Black Mountain

Special faculty meeting on the day the two students return: Straus “incensed,” accuses Frances de Graaff; committee of inquiry (Dreier, Wunsch, Jalowetz, Straus, Sam Brown); Wunsch has persuaded the Asheville Citizen not to reprint the Chattanooga article
The committee unanimously recommends that Anderson leave the community for the summer; Dreier questions her about her sex life (with Addison Bray); a new examination in Asheville is negative

Special faculty meeting: de Graaff contests the sanction; Wunsch and Dreier want to “protect the college”; Molly Gregory, Anni Albers, then Josef Albers (“creates a serious problem in the college”); vote: Anderson must leave for the summer
Faculty meeting: Addison Bray is granted leave to accompany Anderson; they go to the Foremans' (a summer house about 60 miles away); Jeanne Wacker stays for the Music Institute

Letter from ten faculty members to Frances de Graaff: “we can no longer have confidence that you support that kind of education in which we believe,” signed by the Alberses, the Strauses, Dreier, Gregory, Hansgirg, Kurtz, Lowinsky, Herbert Miller
Dreier to the Foremans: the publicity, “even if untrue,” made action unavoidable
Eleanor Roosevelt's “My Day” column: she had hoped to visit the college but could not

Special meeting of the Board of Fellows: the charge extends to Bentley (views “so at variance with essential aims of the College”); Bentley and Foreman have returned; Foreman and the Cohens offer their resignations
Community meeting: statement by Frances de Graaff, who declines reappointment; a guarantee of $1,000 for the following year; Bentley, the Cohens and Foreman also decline reappointment
Community meeting a few days later: the Student Moderator and all the student officers resign; statement by eleven students (later twenty) who leave in protest against the “purge”
Jalowetz to the Board of Fellows: asks to leave the Board; “this amputation”

Wunsch's statement (official report to alumni, parents, Advisory Council): “no one has presented a convincing picture of the causes of the split”; counter-statement by the student officers; statement by another group of students (music, art) in support of the college
John Swackhamer (a former student visiting during the crisis) to the college: “Now it’s just—‘you go’”
Wunsch to Evarts (then October 18, 1944): the young faculty members are to blame, de Graaff “the goat”
Wunsch to J. S. Pittman and Clyde Erwin (GI Bill approval); Herbert Miller to James E. Hillman, July 26, 1945; Dreier to Milton C. Rose, Sept. 1 and Dec. 7, 1945
Kurtz (for the Board) to de Graaff: guarantee of $1,000

From the start of the fall 1944 term, Lowinsky puts integration back on the faculty's agenda; debate on accreditation and local reaction (Straus and Kurtz against); Lowinsky authorized to sound out George Redd (a Fisk sociologist who had already visited with two students)
Roger Sessions to “The Music Editor” (unidentified newspaper clipping)
Evarts (overseas, in the army) to Wunsch: the rector's report reads “like a funeral announcement”
Special faculty meeting: placement tests in English and mathematics, remedial courses; 50-minute classes, no classes after 9:30 p.m.; grades kept but never shown to students
Special faculty meeting: meetings possible without students (Albers, Dreier, Lowinsky; Molly Gregory objects); only the Student Moderator will attend the annual business meeting
Herbert Miller speaks to the whole community on the importance of manners and conventions (“the stuff that binds people together”)

Faculty meeting: individual lists of the “irreducible minimum” (Miller against bare feet, Wunsch against “disordered informality,” Hansgirg, Dreier “no mauling of the opposite sex in public,” Trudi Straus, Molly Gregory); a proposed “standards committee”
Lowinsky to George Redd (Fisk); Redd's reply on December 15, 1944
Wunsch to Forbes: weariness and depression
Dreier to Forbes (new faculty members, Max Dehn)
Student meetings (May 2 and 14, 1945) on the admission of Black students
John Wallen (27, teaching at the University of Maryland, Harvard PhD in psychology) writes Black Mountain a personal letter of application (“this is not the usual kind of application letter”)

Erwin Straus (on leave at Johns Hopkins) meets Wallen in Baltimore and reports to Wunsch (“His speaking voice sounds like tenor but he sings 2d bass”); a second visit to the Wallens; Straus to Herbert Miller (letter and telegram), July 18, 1945: recommends the appointment
Mid-June 1945: Robert Wunsch arrested near Asheville in his roadster with a Marine (“crimes against nature”); he pleads guilty; the charge is reduced to trespassing, suspended sentence
Dreier to Forbes (Dreier on leave in Cambridge)
Lowinsky to the N.A.A.C.P. (June 23), to Mordecai Johnson, president of Howard University (June 27: “proceed a little farther in the summer”), to Abbie Mitchell (July 19, 1945)
Dreier to Forbes on the money to be paid to Wunsch (“an official condoning”)
Albers to Louise Schmidt: the official version (“a slight nervous breakdown”)
Telegram, then letters, from Molly Gregory to Wallen (July 30, August 9, 1945): a one-year appointment
Molly Gregory to Percy H. Baker (Virginia State College)
Wallen to the Steinzors (late July / early August, then August 10, 1945): the visit, “a great counteractive”; the tensions to come
Dreier to Milton Rose (Whitney Foundation) on the Wunsch affair
R. R. Williams, the college's lawyer in Asheville and a member of the Advisory Council, resigns in protest (“counter to… enlightened public opinion in North Carolina”); Dreier's reply, September 1945
Dreier to Norman Fletcher: a fifteen-year building program (125 to 150 students); The Architects’ Collaborative (Cambridge, with Gropius) commissioned for the site plan
Dreier to Mangold: purchase of Wunsch's library
Community meeting on the work program following Wallen's method, in seven groups in the dining hall; Molly Gregory and Bas Allen answer questions; “a lot of laughter and high spirits”

Second community meeting on the work program: a “quite formidable” list (hiring hall, work program seminar, money-making projects: furniture, toys, fabrics, Christmas cards, pottery, greenery, muskrats, log cabins); referred to a planning committee of six chaired by Wallen
Faculty meeting: a Wallen–Levi–Rondthaler committee on decision-making is set up; Albers: “less concern to ‘governing others’, more to learning”
Wallen to Gordon Allport on the “conspiracy of silence” against Otto Rank

The salary-scale file: Dreier to Gregory (March 3, 1946), Rondthaler's memo to the Board (April 15, 1946), Levi's “Preliminary Report” (Dec. 5, 1946), Board meetings of April 23 and August 20, 1946, Clifford Mole to the Board (March 13, 1947), Gregory's statement (March 12, 1947)
Wallen to his parents: the Europeans “can talk democracy”; an account of the meetings on the work program; 17 of the 60 students seen in counseling
Faculty meeting: for 1946-47, one Black faculty member for the year and three or four more Black women students; only one (from Fisk) enrolls
Faculty meeting on the Community Council
Wallen's written statement to the faculty in answer to Albers's suspicions (“to end under-cover rumblings”)
Wallen to Bill Lemman [?]: gives up finishing his Harvard doctorate (“analyzing rather than experiencing”)
Board of Fellows meetings (June 6 and 14, August 29, 1946) on the dormitory designed by The Architects’ Collaborative
Board of Fellows meeting (finances)
Informal study groups: French conversation, shorthand with Rondthaler, history of intentional communities
Levi to Margaret Brown (Wunsch)
Faculty meeting; in March 1947, with Dreier's support, Bill Levi is elected rector
Faculty meeting (finances)
Wallen submits his resignation in mid-March 1947; Levi and Rondthaler ask him to reconsider

Faculty meeting: Hansgirg's term calendar adopted (fall Sept. 22–Feb. 2, spring Feb. 2–June 6, summer June 7–Sept. 20, “study-work” periods, four weeks at Christmas) after a debate on a continuous year (Wallen, M. C. Richards)
Wallen to [?]: “academic chaos”; the Europeans “expect too much; they are unwilling to give enough”
The Board unanimously decides not to renew Niebyl's appointment; a petition by 61 of the 90 students (also signed by Wallen)

Board of Fellows meeting: maximum tuition raised from 1,400 to 1,600 dollars (minimum 500) to remain “an economic cross section of the society”; maintenance and kitchen staff dismissed (saving nearly 4,000 dollars); two students buy the food (80.5 cents a day per person)
Faculty meeting on integration policy

Arthur Penn's proposal to the faculty: an acting class (Stanislavsky), accepted as “informal”; soon also Harry Holl (sculpture) and Jimmie Tite (printing, with a press from government surplus; a second group entrusted to Frank Rice)
Wallen to the Board of Fellows: proposes turning his post into “community development” and allowing a degree in “community service” (fieldwork in the neighboring communities)
Board meeting: a second petition asking for a community meeting on Niebyl is rejected; two notices from the Board to the community on May 9, 1947
Special faculty meeting
A. W. Levi to Maxwell Hahn (integration)
“Report of the Committee of Evaluation” (and a student petition) against the student officers taking part in end-of-term evaluations
Albers to Peter Grippe: terms for the summer guests (room and board, 100 dollars for travel, 25 dollars a week)
Faculty meeting: Albers, absent when Harry Holl's sculpture class (Holl a former pupil of José de Creeft) was authorized, protests; Holl will have to “confer with Albers”
